identity.title: Targeting the provirus in HIV-1 latently infected cells with a cell-activation-inducible CRISPR-Cas9 system: An in vitro proof of concept.

content.abstract: The human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) persists as an integrated provirus in the host cells in a latent state and can reactivate if antiretroviral therapy is interrupted, posing obstacles to an HIV cure. Gene editing technologies can be used to target the provirus. However, several challenges need to be fully addressed, including limiting the nuclease activity to latently infected cells and the possible off-target effects. Here, we provide an in vitro proof-of-principle study to assess the feasibility of a CRISPR/Cas9-based-cell-specific inducible system for the functional inactivation of HIV-1 in latently infected cells. We designed a lentiviral vector expressing the Cas9 nuclease under the nuclear factor of activated T cells (NFAT)-inducible promoter, along with an array of guide RNAs targeting HIV-1-specific genes (gag and tat/rev) and the host chemokine receptor 5 (CCR5), required for viral entry. We demonstrated in different cellular models the inducible expression of the nuclease upon cellular activation and its efficacy in disrupting viral genome and replication. Our findings show the possibility to link Cas9 expression to cellular activation in latently infected cells to reduce the drawbacks of its continuous activity, toward a gene-editing strategy to conditionally inactivate the provirus.
